variants.name: In-process expiry index over steady_clock deadlines
variants.implementation_notes: Standard C++ has no TTL facility, so the receiver keeps an expiry index: each message carries a steady_clock::time_point deadline and a min-heap ordered by deadline (std::priority_queue with std::greater) lets the worker drop everything whose deadline has passed before it dispatches. steady_clock is monotonic and unaffected by wall-clock jumps, which is why it is the right local clock, but its epoch is unspecified and process-local, so the wire value must be an absolute UTC timestamp that each hop converts once. The hand-built index is still justified inside a process - there is no stdlib equivalent of the JMS/AMQP expiry contract - while on an AMQP broker the per-message expiration property is the better enforcement point.
pitfalls: steady_clock's epoch is unspecified (typically boot time) - never serialize it; convert to an absolute UTC deadline at the boundary and accept the bounded skew between hosts.

The heap only exposes expired items when they reach the top, so a long-deadline item at the top delays cleanup of everything behind it; sweep on a timer derived from the earliest deadline instead of only on dequeue.
Calling pop() or top() on an empty std::priority_queue is undefined behaviour, and payloads kept alive in the index must still be released deterministically (move them out or use smart pointers).

variants.name: Broker-enforced per-message expiry property
variants.implementation_notes: When the transport is already AMQP, expiry becomes message metadata instead of application code: publish with the expiration property (a string of milliseconds) or declare x-message-ttl on the queue, and let the broker discard or dead-letter expired messages - route them through a dead-letter exchange so expiry stays observable. This needs no timers in the process, survives restarts and multiple consumers, and is the closest C++ comes to the JMS TTL contract; AMQP 1.0 clients use the ttl header (milliseconds as uint64) instead, and mixing the two dialects silently produces messages that never expire. Choose the in-process index only when there is no broker, or when the check must run on the consumer's own clock.
pitfalls: RabbitMQ evaluates per-message TTL only when a message reaches the queue head, so a large backlog still holds expired payloads and their memory, and dead-lettering strips the original expiration so the message cannot expire again downstream.

The expiration value is a string in AMQP 0-9-1 and a ttl header in milliseconds for AMQP 1.0; passing a number where a string is expected (or the wrong header) silently yields a never-expiring message.
A TTL longer than the queue-level x-message-ttl is capped by the queue, so the effective policy has to be read from the broker configuration, not from the publish call.
